title: Kāṇha's Wedding to Ḍombī
summary: Kāṇha sets out to marry Ḍombī, the Ḍom woman, with a full wedding band: existence and nirvāṇa are his drums, mind and wind his karaṇḍa and cymbals, and the kettledrum sounds amid cries of victory. Married to her, he eats up birth and gains the unsurpassed dharma as dowry; day and night go by in lovemaking, the night passes into dawn in the net of yoginīs, and the yogi who delights in Ḍombī never lets go, drunk on the innate. Munidatta reads Ḍombī first as the unpurified central channel whose flow Kāṇha sets out to break (cp.19.m2), then as the purified avadhūtī, the wisdom seal the yogi never abandons (cp.19.m5).

lines.gloss: rāga (melodic mode) · Bhairavī (name of the rāga)

flags.note: The heading line names only the rāga. The attribution kṛṣṇapādānām ('of Kṛṣṇapāda', that is, Kāṇha), which the manuscript writes just before the song, has been emended out of 1a and I have not added it here; the unit's poet field carries it. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) heading reads b+hai ra bI zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs nag po spyod pa'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the song called Bhairavī, of Kṛṣṇacaryāpāda'. Add '· Kāṇha' if headings should carry the poet.

lines.gloss: existence-and-nirvāṇa (-e: subject, or locative) · paṭaha (drum) · mādala (drum)
lines.en: [Existence and nirvāṇa]{bhava-nirvana} are the [paṭaha]{pataha} and the [mādala]{madala},

flags.note: bhavanirvvāṇe ends in -e, which can mark the subject or a locative. I take it as the subject of an equation (existence and nirvāṇa are the two drums), as Munidatta does ('imagining it as the instruments beginning with the paṭaha', cp.19.m2) and as the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) does (srid dang mya ngan 'das pa pa Ta ha dang rnga bo che). A locative, 'at existence and nirvāṇa, paṭaha and mādala', is possible but gives no clear sense.

lines.translit: maṇa pavaṇa beṇi karaṇḍa kaśālā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: mind · wind · both · karaṇḍa (an instrument; sense uncertain) · kaśālā (cymbals, or a gong) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: [mind and wind]{mana-pavana}, [both]{beni}, are the [karaṇḍa]{karanda} and the [cymbals]{kasala}.

flags.note: karaṇḍa is uncertain: in Sanskrit a basket or box, here apparently a wedding instrument paired with kaśālā; kept in source form as the glossary directs. kaśālā is 'cymbals' per the glossary; a gong is also possible. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) names a single instrument for the pair and adds a verb: yid dang rlung dag gnyis po khar rnga sgrogs par byed, 'mind and wind, the two, sound the bronze drum (khar rnga, probably a gong)'. Munidatta does not gloss either word (cp.19.m2).

lines.gloss: victory · victory · kettledrum · sound · having surged up (absolutive)

flags.note: jaa jaa (Sanskrit jaya jaya) may be a cry raised by the wedding party or the sound the kettledrum itself 'says'. Munidatta lists the cry of 'victory, victory' and the sound of kettledrums as separate omens (cp.19.m2), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) also sets rgyal gyur rgyal gyur apart; I set the cry off in quotation marks.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads rgyal gyur rgyal gyur mkha' la rnga chen sgra, 'Victory! Victory! The sound of the great drum in the sky': 'in the sky' stands where the Bengali has uchaliām̐, 'surging up', perhaps drawn from the commentary's omens in the sky (ākāśe, cp.19.m2). The line keeps the Bengali; 'in the sky' is barred from the line by the dundubhi entry.

lines.gloss: Kāṇha · Ḍombī · for marriage (locative) · set out (past participle) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} has set out for his [marriage]{vivaha} to [Ḍombī]{dombi}.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has kAh+Nas Dom+bi nI ni bag mar blangs, 'Kāṇha took the Ḍombinī as his bride': a completed marriage, where the Bengali caliā has him set out for it.

lines.gloss: Ḍombī · having married (absolutive) · eaten up (past participle in -iu, from āhār- 'eat'; or 'taken away', from ā-hṛ) · birth (janma)
lines.en: Taking [Ḍombī]{dombi} in [marriage]{vivaha}, I have eaten up [birth]{janma};

flags.note: ahāriu jāma. I read jāma as janma, 'birth' (as in the refrain of song 8), and ahāriu as a past participle of āhār-, 'eat' (from āhāra, 'food'; Sanskrit ā-hṛ can also mean 'take away'): birth is eaten up. Munidatta supports birth done away with: 'the faults of arising, perishing and the rest are destroyed' (cp.19.m3), and the Tibetan comment quotes a lemma skye ba'i, 'of birth', with the same gloss. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the line has no 'birth': g.yung mos bag ma len pa'i kha zas sbyar, 'the Ḍom woman prepared the food of the bride-taking', taking ahāriu as āhāra, 'food' (the wedding meal), with Ḍombī as the one who acts. I follow the Bengali and Munidatta; 'eaten up' keeps the food sense the Tibetan heard in the word. Plainer alternative: 'I have done away with birth'.

No subject is expressed: vivāhiā is an absolutive and ahāriu a past participle. I supply 'I' because Munidatta ends his gloss on this couplet 'by me, Kṛṣṇācārya' (mayā kṛṣṇācāryeṇa, cp.19.m3). 'He' (continuing the Kāṇha of 2b) or a passive ('Ḍombī wed, birth is eaten up') are possible; the Tibetan line makes the Ḍom woman the agent (g.yung mos).

lines.gloss: as dowry (locative) · made (past participle) · unsurpassed (anuttara) · dharma · (refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: kia is literally 'made' ('the unsurpassed dharma was made the dowry'); I render the sense, 'gained as dowry'. Munidatta takes jautuke as an instrumental: 'by the dowry, without affliction, the unsurpassed Dharma was directly realized by me' (cp.19.m3). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has no verb: zhal mthong ston mo bla med chos nyid do, 'the feast of seeing the face is the unsurpassed dharmatā'.
dhāma is read as dharma with Munidatta (anuttaradharma, cp.19.m3) and the Tibetan (chos nyid). Sanskrit dhāman, 'abode, domain', would give 'the unsurpassed abode', which neither witness supports.

lines.gloss: day and night (aharniśi) · in the pursuit of lovemaking (surata-prasaṅga, locative) · goes
lines.en: Day and night go by in [lovemaking]{surata};

flags.note: I take ahiṇisi, 'day and night', as the subject of jāa, 'goes', parallel to raeṇi pohāa in 4b. It can also be adverbial with an unstated person as subject ('day and night he goes on in lovemaking'); Munidatta speaks of the lord of yogis who is attached to lovemaking day and night (cp.19.m4).

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nyin mtshan shin tu dga' ba'i grogs dang 'grogs, 'day and night he keeps company with the companion of great delight': it takes suraa as su-rata, 'great delight' (shin tu dga' ba), and -pasaṅge as saṅga, 'companion' (grogs). I keep the Bengali surata, 'lovemaking', as Munidatta does (suratābhiṣvaṅga, cp.19.m4).

lines.gloss: in the net of yoginīs (locative) · night · passes, turns to dawn · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: in the [net of yoginīs]{yoginijala} the [night]{rajani} passes into dawn.

flags.note: pohāa is said of the night coming to its end at daybreak (compare later Bengali rāt pohāno); I render 'passes into dawn'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees: nams langs gyur, 'dawn broke'.

lines.gloss: of Ḍombī · with, in company · who · yogi · enamoured, delighting (rakta)

flags.note: jo joi is read as 'the yogi who' (jo, relative 'who'; joi, yogī). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has kye'i Dom+bi grogs dang gang gang dga', 'O Ḍombī, whoever delights in your company': a vocative, and gang gang, 'whoever', with no word for 'yogi', as if reading jo jo. Munidatta has both: 'whichever yogins (ye ye yoginaḥ) delight in attachment to lovemaking with her' (cp.19.m5).

lines.translit: khaṇaha na chāṛaa sahaja unmatto || dhru ||
lines.gloss: even for a moment (kṣaṇa with emphatic -ha) · not · leaves, lets go · innate · maddened, drunk (unmatta) · (refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: does not let go for even a moment, [drunk]{matta} on the [innate]{sahaja}.

flags.note: unmatto (Sanskrit unmatta) is properly 'maddened, out of one's mind'; the glossary lists it under matta with the rendering 'drunk', which I use. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lhan cig skyes pas myos, 'intoxicated by the innate', which supports 'drunk'. 'Mad with the innate' is the alternative. The object of 'let go' (Ḍombī, or her company) is unstated in the Bengali and left unstated here.

notes.text: Munidatta introduces the song as another caryā spoken by Kṛṣṇācārya 'to make that same meaning firm', presumably the meaning of the song before it, also Kāṇha's (cp.19.m1). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has instead 'Kṛṣṇacaryāpāda, who teaches the meaning of reality (de kho na nyid kyi don), spoke another song', as if reading tattvārtha for tam evārtham.

Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music; each song is headed by the rāga it is sung to. Bhairavī is the rāga here (the word is also a goddess's name). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) transcribes the name, b+hai ra bI, where for song 12, also in Bhairavī, the glossary records rnga bo che, 'great drum'.

The paṭaha and the mādala are both drums. The paṭaha (Old Bengali paṛaha) is beaten in processions, festivals and public proclamations; the mādala (from Sanskrit mardala) is a two-headed barrel drum played with the hands. Here they lead the wedding band. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) keeps pa Ta ha and renders mādala as rnga bo che, 'great drum'.

karaṇḍa is kept in source form: in Sanskrit it is a basket or box, and here it seems to name a wedding instrument beside kaśālā, a bell-metal percussion instrument (compare Sanskrit kāṃsyatāla, 'bell-metal cymbal'). beṇi, 'both', follows the pair mind and wind; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) agrees (yid dang rlung dag gnyis po, 'mind and wind, the two') but names one instrument, khar rnga, 'bronze drum', and adds a verb, sgrogs par byed, 'sound out'.

Shastri prints ধ্রু, the cue to sing the refrain again, after this line too, although the refrain is couplet 2 and the cue otherwise follows the refrain and the later couplets. Munidatta's count, in which couplet 3 is his 'second verse' (cp.19.m3), confirms couplet 2 as the refrain. The cue is not translated.

Munidatta reads existence and nirvāṇa as the conceptual thought of mind, wind and the rest, spoken of before, which is to be purified in sequence: the yogi imagines (utprekṣya) it as the instruments beginning with the paṭaha and takes great bliss as his companion (cp.19.m2). Where the Sanskrit has 'conceptual thought' (vikalpa), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the comment has 'nonconceptual' (rnam par mi rtog pa), and it takes bhāṇḍa, 'instrument', in its other sense, 'vessel' (snod).

A wedding procession: the groom sets out for the bride's house with drums, cymbals and cries of victory. The bride is Ḍombī, a woman of the Ḍom caste, whom caste society treated as untouchable; to marry her openly, with a band and acclamation, flouts every rule of caste purity. The song keeps the scene literal.

jaa jaa is Sanskrit jaya jaya, 'victory! victory!', the cry of acclamation at festivals and triumphs; dunduhi is the dundubhi, a large kettledrum; sāda is śabda, 'sound'. uchaliām̐, 'having surged up', is an absolutive: the sound swells as Kāṇha sets out.

Munidatta reads Ḍombī here as the channel of semen (śukranāḍikā), the unpurified avadhūtikā, and says that Kṛṣṇācārya set out 'to break her flow' (vāhavabhaṅgārtham) where the song has him set out for the wedding (vivāhe), apparently hearing vi-vāha as the stopping of a flow; then omens appeared in abundance in the sky: cries of 'victory, victory', a rain of flowers, the sound of kettledrums and the like (cp.19.m2). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the comment has 'to destroy her leaking' ('dzag pa gzhom pa'i phyir). The song celebrates a marriage; the commentary makes the marriage a breaking. The two are left side by side.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads kAh+Nas Dom+bi nI ni bag mar blangs, 'Kāṇha took the Ḍombinī as his bride', a marriage already made, where the Bengali caliā has him only set out for it.

jāma is Old Bengali for janma, 'birth', one life in the round of rebirth, as in the refrain of song 8. ahāriu has the past-participle ending -iu; I take it from āhār-, 'eat', a verb made from āhāra, 'food', though Sanskrit ā-hṛ also means 'take away, remove'. Either way birth is done with. Munidatta paraphrases 'the faults of arising, perishing and the rest are destroyed' (utpādabhaṅgādidoṣā nāśitāḥ), just after a phrase whose link to the song's words is unclear, 'having made a breaking, victory' (bhaṅgaṃ kṛtvā jayam) (cp.19.m3). 'Eaten up' keeps the sense of food that the Tibetan translation heard in the word.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads the line g.yung mos bag ma len pa'i kha zas sbyar, 'the Ḍom woman (g.yung mo) prepared the food of the bride-taking', that is, the wedding meal. It takes ahāriu as āhāra, 'food', makes Ḍombī the agent, and has nothing for jāma, 'birth'. Yet the Tibetan comment on the couplet quotes a lemma skye ba'i, 'of birth', and explains it as destroying the faults of birth, perishing and the rest, as Munidatta's Sanskrit does (cp.19.m3): the translators' commentary knew 'birth' even where their verse has 'food'. The translation follows the Bengali.

Munidatta introduces this couplet, his 'second verse', as stating the fruit of the marriage with Ḍombī. Here Ḍombī has the form of wind (vāyurūpā), and the marriage is the vivāha of her 'door of going' (gamanadvāra), which the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) explains as destroying her going through that door. With the faults of arising and perishing destroyed, 'by the dowry, without affliction, the unsurpassed Dharma was directly realized by me, Kṛṣṇācārya' (cp.19.m3). akleśena can also mean simply 'without trouble'; the Tibetan takes it as 'free of afflictions' (nyon mongs pa med pa).

jautuka (Sanskrit yautuka) is the property that comes with a bride. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) renders it zhal mthong ston mo, apparently 'the feast of seeing the face', a wedding feast at which the bride's face is first seen, and dharma as chos nyid, 'the nature of things': zhal mthong ston mo bla med chos nyid do, 'the feast of seeing the face is the unsurpassed dharmatā'. With 'food' in 3a, the Tibetan makes the whole couplet a wedding feast.

The net of yoginīs: in the yoginī tantras the female deities of a maṇḍala are pictured as a net or circle around its lord. The couplet stays with the wedding night: day and night given to love, and the night ending at dawn among the yoginīs.

Munidatta introduces this couplet, his 'third verse', as stating the power of the yoginī. The lord of yogis is attached day and night to lovemaking with 'this [jñānamudrā]{jnanamudra}', the wisdom seal; the net of yoginīs is his rays of knowledge (jñānaraśmi); the passing of the night is the flight of the darkness of the afflictions. He then quotes a scriptural verse: when the blessed lord of breath has dissolved into the self alone, and the in- and out-breaths are gone and the life-wind is stilled and held, a spreading light, most radiant, issues from the yogis' own bodies, destroys darkness and pervades the three worlds (cp.19.m4). Where the Sanskrit has jñānamudrā, the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) of the comment has ye shes kyi rgya mtsho, 'ocean of knowledge', as if reading samudra.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads nyin mtshan shin tu dga' ba'i grogs dang 'grogs, 'day and night he keeps company with the companion of great delight', taking suraa as su-rata, 'very delightful', and -pasaṅge as saṅga, 'companion'. Munidatta's paraphrase keeps lovemaking: suratābhiṣvaṅga, 'attachment to lovemaking' (cp.19.m4).

Munidatta introduces the last couplet, his 'fourth verse', as the conduct of the lord of yogis through the yoginī's grace. Here Ḍombī is the jñānamudrā, the purified avadhūtikā, luminous by nature; the yogins who delight in attachment to lovemaking with her never give her up even for a moment, because she is the support of the joy of great bliss. He ends with the opening words of a verse of Saraha, 'when the mind has gone to the absence of all things…' (cp.19.m5). In his comment on couplet 1 the same Ḍombī was the unpurified avadhūtikā whose flow Kāṇha set out to break (cp.19.m2), and on couplet 3 she had the form of wind (cp.19.m3): his reading of her shifts within the song.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads kye'i Dom+bi grogs dang gang gang dga', 'O Ḍombī, whoever delights in your company': it addresses Ḍombī and has gang gang, 'whoever', where the Bengali has jo joi, 'the yogi who'. Munidatta's gloss has both the distributive and the yogins: 'whichever yogins (ye ye yoginaḥ) delight' (cp.19.m5).

The last couplet is marked as the bhaṇitā, but the poet does not name himself in it, and the Tibetan line has no name either. Its yogi is general ('the yogi who…'), though a listener may hear Kāṇha in him.

sahaja unmatto: 'maddened (or drunk) with the innate'. Sanskrit unmatta is 'out of one's mind'; the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lhan cig skyes pas myos, 'intoxicated by the innate'. khaṇaha is kṣaṇa, 'moment', with an emphatic ending: 'even for a moment'.

proposals.definition: Attachment, clinging (abhiṣvaṅga). Usually a fault, as when Munidatta calls attachment to māyā delusion; in his comments on yogic union it is positive: the lord of yogis is attached day and night to lovemaking with the jñānamudrā (cp.19.m4), whom the yogins never give up (cp.19.m5). Tibetan: mngon par 'grogs pa, mngon par chags pa.
proposals.rationale: A recurring word of Munidatta's commentary: twice in this song (suratābhiṣvaṅga), and, as the glossary's entries for the ocean of illusion and the vajra woman record, in songs 15 and 18. One English word for it keeps the woven commentary consistent and shows its double use, a fault toward māyā and a virtue in union. The surata entry already lists the compound; the two entries would both match it, which is correct.

questions: 3a: I read ahāriu jāma as 'I have eaten up birth' (jāma = janma, with Munidatta and the Tibetan comment's lemma skye ba'i, 'of birth'), against the Tibetan line's 'the Ḍom woman prepared the food of the bride-taking' (kha zas). Do you accept 'eaten up', or prefer the plainer 'done away with' (if ahāriu is from ā-hṛ, 'take away')?
Couplet 3 names no subject. I supplied 'I' from Munidatta's 'by me, Kṛṣṇācārya' (cp.19.m3), which makes a shift from 'Kāṇha has set out' in 2b. Keep 'I', or use 'he' or a passive?
3b: kia is literally 'made'. I wrote 'as dowry I have gained the unsurpassed dharma'. Would you prefer the more literal 'the unsurpassed dharma was made the dowry'?
The approved rendering of vivaha is the noun 'marriage', which forced 'set out for his marriage to Ḍombī' (2b) and 'Taking Ḍombī in marriage' (3a). Could 'marry' or 'wed' be added as variants?
5b: unmatta is properly 'maddened'; the glossary lists it under matta, 'drunk'. I used 'drunk on the innate' (the Tibetan myos supports it). Should the entry take 'mad' as a variant for unmatta?

Heading: the heading line has only the rāga; the attribution kṛṣṇapādānām was emended out of 1a, and I did not add the poet. Should headings carry '· Kāṇha' (or 'Kṛṣṇapāda', as the brief's 'Lūyīpāda' example suggests)?

Glossary matching: the bhairavi entry lists rnga bo che among its Tibetan forms, so the Tibetan of 1a, where rnga bo che renders the mādala, is reported as a bhairavi hit. The same form is listed under madala and dundubhi. Should it be dropped from bhairavi, or limited to headings?
Couplet 5 is marked as the bhaṇitā, but the poet does not name himself in it (nor in the Tibetan). Keep the marking?

1b: 'mind and wind, both, are the karaṇḍa and the cymbals' keeps beṇi after the pair, as the Bengali and the Tibetan (gnyis po) have it, but it reads stiffly. Acceptable, or would you drop the commas or rephrase?
